body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about StrongLifts comes from its App Store listing, its website and support pages, and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

StrongLifts hasn't gone anywhere, and its 5×5 is the same program. What changed is the price of entry: there's no free tier anymore, and the Power Pack many long-time lifters bought years ago no longer covers the app. Here's how that happened, in StrongLifts' own words, then every realistic place to run your next 5×5, free ones included.

What happened to StrongLifts, year by year

StrongLifts' support article on Power Pack, last updated October 7, 2026, lays out the history:

  • 2010 to 2014: the app is free, with nothing for sale.
  • 2014: Power Pack arrives, a one-time $9.99 add-on for warm-ups, the plate calculator and assistance work. Logging your 5×5 stays free.
  • May 2018: Power Pack sales stop and a Pro subscription begins. New features go into Pro, not Power Pack.
  • June 2020: a Pro Lifetime plan is added: all of Pro, no recurring fee, at a higher price.
  • 2023: the app starts calling Power Pack "lifetime." The support article now says that wording was a mistake, and that Power Pack was never a lifetime purchase of the whole app.
  • 2025: Power Pack is retired and the free tier ends. The app is Pro only, and Power Pack owners get 50% off their first year.
  • Now: the App Store listing says StrongLifts is "free to download, but requires a subscription to use," with a 7-day trial on the yearly plan only.

StrongLifts' stated reason is that hosting, development and support are ongoing costs a one-time purchase doesn't cover. Of 317 App Store reviews at one to three stars from August 2025 to November 2026, 259 mention price or the subscription and 101 mention lifetime or Power Pack. Most are from 2026, and several describe meeting the paywall after a recent update, though the support article dates the change to 2025.

Your options, in short

  • Stay with StrongLifts if you want this exact program run for you, with automatic deloads and an Apple Watch app. Pro is $59.99 a year, and Power Pack owners can ask for 50% off the first year.
  • Go free with Boostcamp or a spreadsheet if you're happy to work out each new weight yourself.
  • Switch to Kiron if you want a 5×5 that fills in your next weight, programs to move on to when it stalls, and runs in the same plan, for {{kiron:price-annual}}. It has no Watch app, no automatic deloads and no StrongLifts import.

Whichever you pick, export your StrongLifts history first. It takes a minute, even from behind the paywall.

Stay and pay: what StrongLifts costs now

If StrongLifts was working for you, paying is a reasonable answer: it plans the program, weights and schedule for you.On the US App Store, Pro costs $4.99 weekly, $11.99 monthly, $29.99 quarterly or $59.99 yearly, and two five-year plans are listed at $199.99 and $239.99. Only the yearly plan has a free trial (7 days). To pay monthly, StrongLifts' help article suggests starting the yearly trial, cancelling before day 7, then switching to monthly in Settings.

  • Power Pack owners get 50% off the first year. Email StrongLifts a copy of your old invoice, or contact them through the app if you've lost it. Your history comes back once the subscription starts.
  • Ask before you buy a long plan. The support article says the 2020 Pro Lifetime plan is still offered, but the US App Store lists the five-year plans and nothing named lifetime. If paying once matters, ask StrongLifts which one you're getting.

StrongLifts is the better fit if you want:

  • one program, set up for you, with nothing to decide
  • deloads handled for you: it lowers the weight after repeated misses (you set when and by how much, for example 15% after two failed attempts) and suggests starting lighter after a break
  • small jumps, down to 1 lb every three workouts with fractional plates
  • an Apple Watch app, rebuilt in version 4.4.0 in October 2026

Run it free: Boostcamp, a notebook or a spreadsheet

A 5×5 doesn't strictly need an app. The rules fit on an index card: three sessions a week, two workouts taking turns, add weight when you get all your reps, repeat the weight when you don't, and take some off if you keep missing.

Boostcamp's free tier has no time limit and includes its tracker, warm-up templates, a custom program builder and 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs. Its 5×5 page lists community-uploaded 5×5 programs as free. The catch: Auto Progression, which handles linear progression and missed reps, is part of Pro, and the free plate calculator stops after 10 uses, so you choose each new weight yourself. Pro is $59.99 a year with a 7-day trial, or $14.99 a month.

A notebook or a spreadsheet works too: log every set and mark the lifts where you got all your reps, so you know what goes up next time. The friction is logging between sets on a phone. Our honest comparison of spreadsheets and workout apps covers the trade-off, and for a program as simple as a 5×5, the sheet holds up well.

Move to Kiron: Beginner 5×5 and Novice Linear Progression

Kiron (that's us) is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}}. Two of its 36 ready-made programs cover the same ground. They're Kiron's own programs, built on the classic beginner barbell structure:

  • Beginner 5×5. Workout A is squat 5×5, bench press 5×5 and barbell row 5×5. Workout B is squat 5×5, overhead press 5×5 and deadlift 1×5. The two take turns three days a week, so on the Monday, Wednesday and Friday Kiron suggests, you get A, B, A one week and B, A, B the next. It's ongoing, listed at 45 minutes a session, and needs a barbell and a rack.
  • Novice Linear Progression. Workout A is squat 3×5, overhead press 3×5 and deadlift 1×5. Workout B is squat 3×5, bench press 3×5 and power clean 5×3, plus optional chin-ups for 3 sets of 5 to 10. If you're new to cleans, the app suggests barbell rows 3×5 until you learn the movement. Same rotation, listed at 60 minutes.

To start one, tap Add a program, then Choose a preset program, and open it. Under Your training days, tap the days you train; the page says your workouts run in order on those days and shows which comes first. Pick fewer than three and it warns that the program will run slower than planned. Then tap Start this program.

How the weight goes up

Your first session starts with empty weight boxes, because Kiron can't read your StrongLifts history. Type the weights you were lifting, a little lighter after time off. From then on, Kiron fills in every set:

  • Every set hit its reps: next time is 5 lb heavier, or 2.5 kg if you lift in kilograms, and the card says so: "You hit every set, so we added 5 lb."
  • Reps to spare: after an exercise's last set, Kiron asks "How many more reps could you have done?" Answer 3 or more and the next jump is about 5% of the weight, in whole steps, so a 200 lb squat goes to 210 lb.
  • Squats every session: the squat is in both workouts and shares one history, so it goes up every session. The other lifts go up each time their workout comes around.
  • A missed rep: if any set falls short, or you log fewer sets than planned, the weight stays the same.
  • A stall: Kiron has no automatic deload. If you keep missing, type a lighter weight yourself. StrongLifts does this for you, and it's a real difference.

Around the sets, Kiron lists warm-up sets for the main lifts (the empty bar, then about 40%, 60% and 80% of your first work set) and shows the plates for each side under the set you're about to load. A missed workout shows on Today with options to move it, pick a day or skip it. If you run too, runs go in the same plan and calendar; our post on fitting real lifting around Runna shows a week of both.

Where Kiron falls short: it has no Apple Watch app and reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect afterwards; the step up is fixed, not adjustable; it imports history only from Fitbod, Strong and Hevy files; it can't export your history; it needs a connection to open a workout; and it's new, where StrongLifts has a long track record with this one program.

After 5×5 stalls: what to run next

Everyone on a 5×5 stalls eventually. The standard moves work in any app or none: take about 10% off the stalled lift and build back up, do fewer sets (three sets of five instead of five), or move to a program that adds weight weekly or once a cycle instead of every session. If you stay with StrongLifts, its intermediate 5×5 and Madcow templates are the next step there. In Kiron, three programs pick up where Beginner 5×5 leaves off:

  • Wave Loading Strength (three days): two main lifts a session, worked up through percentages of a training max to a top set of as many good reps as you can, then 5×5 at a lighter weight. The percentages change over a 3-week cycle, from 65 to 85% in week one up to 95% in week three, and Kiron turns them into real weights from the training max you enter. The cycle's last workout reminds you to raise the maxes: 5 lb (2.5 kg) for bench and press, 10 lb (5 kg) for squat and deadlift.
  • Upper / Lower Strength (four days): a heavy squat day, a heavy deadlift day, a heavy bench and press day, and a lighter upper day. The heavy lifts stay at 3 to 5 reps and go up a little when you finish every rep of every set.
  • Push / Pull / Legs (six days): for when muscle is the main goal, with each day opening on a heavy compound lift before higher-rep accessories.

Kiron matches lifts by exercise, so your squat history comes along and the new starting weights pick up where you left off. Found a program elsewhere? Paste it under Import a plan. And if your next plan runs in blocks, see our guide to following a multi-phase plan without a coach.

Take your StrongLifts history with you

StrongLifts' export help article, updated October 17, 2026, gives two ways to save your log:

  • From the app: Settings, then Export Data, then Share to email yourself a CSV file.
  • Stuck on the paywall: tap the menu icon at the top right, tap Contact Support, and send the pre-filled email to your own address. The CSV comes with it.

The file opens in any spreadsheet, so keep it. Our guide to exporting workout history covers five other apps too. Kiron can't import it: if you switch, type your current working weights into your first session and Kiron takes it from there.

StrongLifts and Kiron are from the US App Store's purchase list on November 15, 2026; Boostcamp's list doesn't name plan lengths, so its prices come from its own pricing page. Questions people ask about StrongLifts

Is StrongLifts still free?

No. Its support article says the app has been Pro only since 2025, and the App Store listing says it needs a subscription. New users get a 7-day trial on the yearly plan.

Is there a StrongLifts lifetime plan?

StrongLifts' support article says its Pro Lifetime plan from June 2020 is still offered. On November 15, 2026, the US App Store's purchase list showed five-year plans at $199.99 and $239.99, and nothing named lifetime. Ask StrongLifts which plan you're buying before you pay.

Is there a free 5×5 app?

Boostcamp's free tier lists community-uploaded 5×5 programs and has no time limit, but automatic progression is part of Pro, so you set each new weight yourself. A notebook or spreadsheet works too. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Is StrongLifts good for beginners?

It's built for them. The App Store listing says it's made for lifters starting or returning to barbell training, and the app plans every set and weight. The open question is the price, not the program.

If StrongLifts' price is why you're here and you want a 5×5 that still fills in your next weight, start Kiron's Beginner 5×5 with your current weights. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron. If you'd rather not pay anyone, Boostcamp's free tier or a spreadsheet will run a 5×5 fine, as long as you add the weight yourself. And if StrongLifts' deloads and Watch app are what you'd miss, staying is a fair call.
